data.text:
DMK's Dalit massacre over a 30 rupees wage hike demand by Dalit tea estate workers.

The Manjolai Massacre, also known as the Thamirabarani Massacre, occurred on July 23, 1999, in Tirunelveli, Tamil Nadu, due to a violent police response to a peaceful protest by tea estate workers. The workers, primarily Dalits employed by the Bombay Burmah Trading Corporation (BBTC) at the Manjolai tea estates, were demanding better wages, improved working conditions, and the release of 652 workers arrested during an earlier protest on June 8, 1999. The earlier arrests followed a demonstration against wage cuts and poor labor conditions, including a demand to include travel time to work sites in their working hours.

On July 23, approximately 4,000–5,000 workers and supporters, organized by groups like Puthiya Tamilagam, Tamil Manila Congress, and Communist parties, marched to the Tirunelveli Collectorate to submit a petition. The procession, starting from the Tirunelveli railway station, was stopped about 50 meters from the Collectorate. An altercation with the police led to a lathi charge, during which police attacked the marchers with batons and, according to some accounts, threw stones. As the crowd fled in panic, many were driven toward the Thamirabarani River, where 17 people, including two women and a two-year-old child, drowned while attempting to escape. Reports also indicate injuries to others, including media personnel.

The underlying causes included long-standing labor disputes with BBTC, which leased the 8,374-acre estate and was accused of imposing wage penalties and denying benefits. The workers’ demands for fair pay (e.g., a wage hike to Rs 150 per day) and better conditions were unmet, fueling tensions. Some sources suggest the police action was unprovoked, with Human Rights Watch condemning it as a brutal attack on Dalit workers. Political figures like TMC president G.K. Moopanar alleged the violence was orchestrated for electoral gains in 1999, though this claim remains contentious. The state government, led by Chief Minister Karunanidhi, claimed the marchers initiated violence, a narrative disputed by activists and eyewitnesses who described the protest as peaceful.

The massacre highlighted systemic issues like caste-based oppression, as most victims were Dalits, and inadequate labor protections in Tamil Nadu’s tea estates. Despite investigations and calls for justice, including demands for a judicial inquiry and fresh post-mortems, no significant accountability was achieved, and the workers’ demands largely remained unaddressed.

The victims included a 16 month old child.

data.text:
Aktuell ist wieder von dramatisch steigenden Meeresspiegeln die Rede. Ein Inselstaat verklagt Industrieländer vor dem Internationalen Gerichtshof in Den Haag – angeblich, weil er im Meer zu versinken droht. Doch bei allem Verständnis für die Sorgen kleiner Inselstaaten: Die Diskussion ist oft einseitig und wissenschaftlich unpräzise.

Fakt ist: Der globale Meeresspiegel ist in den letzten 100 Jahren um etwa 20 bis 25 Zentimeter gestiegen – das sind rund 1,5 bis 2 mm pro Jahr im langjährigen Durchschnitt. Seit den 1990er Jahren hat sich der Anstieg beschleunigt – auf etwa 3,5 mm pro Jahr laut Satellitenmessungen.
🔗 Quelle: NASA Sea Level Change
🔗 Quelle: IPCC 2021, Summary for Policymakers (AR6) (S. 9, Abb. SPM.1)

Was in der Debatte oft völlig übersehen wird: Viele Inseln und Küsten sinken zusätzlich, unabhängig vom Meeresspiegel, z. B. durch:
•Tektonische Verschiebungen (Plattenbewegungen, Subduktion etc.)
•Isostatische Prozesse (Nachwirkungen der letzten Eiszeit)
•Absinken durch Grundwasserentnahme (z. B. in Jakarta oder Manila)
•Korallenrückgang durch lokale Umweltveränderungen

🔗 Quelle: US Geological Survey zur Landabsenkung
🔗 Quelle: Nature: “Land subsidence will exacerbate climate change-related flooding in Jakarta”

Beispiel Jakarta: Die Stadt versinkt stellenweise bis zu 10 cm pro Jahr – nicht wegen des Klimawandels, sondern wegen exzessiver Wasserentnahme aus dem Boden.
🔗 Quelle: BBC: “Jakarta is sinking”

Viele pazifische Inseln liegen auf instabilen tektonischen Platten und sind von Natur aus geologisch gefährdet. Trotzdem wird in Medien und NGOs häufig nur „der Klimawandel“ als Ursache genannt – oft ohne geologische Einordnung.

⸻

Fazit:

✅ Der Meeresspiegel steigt messbar, aber nicht dramatisch schnell.
✅ Lokale Effekte wie Erdbewegungen oder Grundwassersenkungen spielen oft eine größere Rolle als der Klimawandel selbst.
✅ Die politische Darstellung in den Medien ist häufig undifferenziert.
✅ Die Klage vor dem Internationalen Gerichtshof ist symbolisch motiviert, nicht durch eindeutige wissenschaftliche Belege getragen.

data.text:
Read and share as you like 😊🙏

I agree, Sen. Lacson. So now you're beginning to see who’s really the “friend” of the Filipino people and Republic of the Philippines, then?

Let’s get one thing straight: what happened between President Marcos Jr. and Trump wasn't a diplomatic meeting or a meeting per se. It was a summons. A parade of submission. A master-servant performance on the global stage. And what did we get in return? A paltry 1% tariff reduction?  Yes, from 20% to 19%, in exchange for a bonanza of trade (zero tariff for American goods entering the Philippines) and military concessions all tilted in favor of the United States. That’s NOT diplomacy. That’s daylight geopolitical robbery dressed in “ironclad” rhetoric.

And please, let’s not pretend it stopped at tariffs. Marcos Jr. practically turned the archipelago into a floating fortress for Uncle Sam. Nine EDCA sites, US missile deployment, an ammunition hub in the works. It’s as if we’re begging to be dragged into someone else’s war.

Let’s call it what it is: neo-colonialism, neo-imperialism, and yes, neo-extractivism, — the 21st-century way of bleeding a country dry, not just of minerals, but of dignity, sovereignty, and independent thought and strategic autonomy!

And the cherry on top? Trump couldn’t help but take a swipe at former President Duterte, a dig that was not only unnecessary, unethical, and uncalled for but strategically humiliating. Marcos Jr. just stood there, possibly smiling. Was that diplomacy, or was that defeat?

So now, Mr. President, where to turn to? China? But take note, you betrayed China BIG TIME! Our foreign policy is subservient and heavily leaning and under the thumb of Uncle Sam, with deployment of US missile systems, staging an ammunition hub, 9 EDCA sites (US military bases), and de facto betraying the One-China Policy/Principle among others. Just to repeat and re-emphasize. 

After all the betrayals, it seems that you’ve burned that bridge with a flamethrower, Mr. President!

ASEAN? Most of our Southeast Asian neighbors are growing visibly uneasy with your confrontational and belligerent antics in our dispute over the South China Sea with China. Note that our ASEAN neighbors are not looking for war games. They're looking for stability, security, and peace. 

So, you're now stuck in a geopolitical limbo, Mr. President, a pawn with delusions of being a player.

So, what do you think you should do? First step: clean the house. Fire the cabinet bootlickers who can’t think beyond Washington’s talking points. Replace them with Filipinos who understand nuance, strategic balance, and the concept of national interest, sovereignty, and independent foreign policy. 

But therein lies another dilemma; those qualified, of course, not all, are allied with the Vice President, your so-called “mortal enemy.” So, you’re caught between an incompetent inner circle and a competent opposition within the ambit of the Vice President. Bravo! Good luck to that Mr. President! 

Folks, in the end, this is what happens when national leadership confuses performative patriotism with actual statecraft, and foreign allegiance with strategic partnership.

Good luck, Mr. President. You’ll need it. And more importantly, the country needs a miracle, or at the very least, a spine.

To the Filipino people, please wake up… are you still sleeping? Time to wake up, folks!

CSAFP’s CORNER | GUARDIANS IN UNIFORM, RESPONDERS AT HEART

In his latest Inquirer column, “The General Idea,” Armed Forces of the Philippines (AFP) Chief of Staff General Romeo S Brawner Jr. underscored the AFP’s pivotal role in disaster response operations—proving that the military’s duty to protect goes beyond combat, reaching every Filipino in times of crisis.

Emphasizing the AFP’s unwavering commitment to humanitarian assistance and disaster response (HADR), General Brawner noted that Filipino soldiers are mobilized even before disasters strike, prepared to confront nature’s wrath with the same courage, discipline, and resolve they bring to the frontlines.

“This July alone, the country has experienced widespread flooding due to the Habagat and successive typhoons. Even before Tropical Storm Crising made landfall, our troops were already activated,” he wrote.

Key AFP units including the 525th Engineer Combat Battalion, 505th Search and Rescue Group, and the Naval Combat Engineering Brigade (Seabees) were among the first to deploy—clearing roads, reinforcing infrastructure, conducting evacuations, and delivering aid to affected areas. Reservists, many of whom are civilian professionals, also answered the call without hesitation or compensation.

General Brawner recounted past missions, notably the multinational coordination he led during Super Typhoon Yolanda in 2013, and more recent international humanitarian deployments to Turkey in 2023 and Myanmar in April 2025. These missions, he said, reflect the AFP’s outward-looking, compassionate spirit.

“Time and again, I have seen our troops wade through floods, rappel down cliffs, and carry children to safety. There’s no bonus for this. No medal can fully capture its worth. But we do it anyway—because this is what it means to serve,” General Brawner stated.

As the nation confronts the escalating threats of climate change and increasingly complex emergencies, General Brawner assured the public that the Armed Forces is modernizing not only its warfighting capabilities, but also its capacity to save lives.

CSAFP reaffirmed that in moments of disaster—when storms strike, the ground trembles, or hope begins to fade—Filipino soldiers will always stand ready. Through every rescue mission, relief effort, and life saved, the AFP lives out its core duty to serve and protect.

“We are not just peacekeepers and defenders,” General Brawner declared. “We are guardians in uniform, responders at heart.”
